options.a: Replace shipping papers for loads under 1,001 pounds
options.b: Communicate the hazard of materials on a vehicle
options.c: Identify the shipper and receiver for the load
options.d: Mark the packing group of each package on board

distractorExplanations.a: Shipping papers are required for hazmat shipments either way; 1,001 lb is the Table 2 placarding threshold, not a paper exemption.
distractorExplanations.c: Shipper and consignee details appear on the shipping papers; placards show the hazard class of what is aboard.
distractorExplanations.d: Packing group is shown on shipping papers; placards communicate hazard class on the vehicle exterior.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-classes-placa.explanation: Placards provide hazard communication; shipping papers remain required documentation. Placards inform emergency responders and the public.

options.a: One-digit hazard class number
options.b: Three-digit ERG guide number
options.c: Four-digit packing group code
options.d: Four-digit UN/NA number

distractorExplanations.a: The hazard class (1–9) appears in the placard's bottom corner, but the ID number is a separate four-digit UN/NA code.
distractorExplanations.b: ERG guide numbers are three digits; the ID number on papers and placards is the four-digit UN/NA number.
distractorExplanations.c: Packing groups are Roman numerals I, II or III; the four-digit number is the UN/NA identification number.

options.a: Set the placarding thresholds for each hazard class
options.b: List the segregation table rules for loading incompatible classes
options.c: Provide initial isolation/evacuation and fire/spill guidance
options.d: Record the shipper's 24-hour emergency phone contact

distractorExplanations.a: Placarding tables are in 49 CFR 172.504; the ERG gives first-response actions, not placarding rules.
distractorExplanations.b: Segregation rules are in 49 CFR 177.848; the ERG guides initial emergency response to incidents.
distractorExplanations.d: The 24-hour emergency response number appears on shipping papers; the ERG provides generic initial response guidance.

options.a: A load includes any Table 1 material such as explosives
options.b: A single bulk package of one hazard class is aboard
options.c: 2,205 pounds or more of one Table 2 category is loaded at one facility
options.d: Non-bulk packages of two or more hazard categories require placarding

distractorExplanations.a: Table 1 materials (Divisions 1.1–1.3, poison gas, etc.) need their own placards; the Dangerous placard cannot replace them.
distractorExplanations.b: The Dangerous placard option covers non-bulk packages of two or more Table 2 categories, not a single bulk package.
distractorExplanations.c: At 2,205 lb (1,000 kg) or more of one category loaded at one facility, that class's own placard is required instead.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-classes-placa.explanation: Dangerous placard rules are specific aggregation/placarding table exceptions—not a universal substitute. It may then replace separate Table 2 placards.

options.a: Proper shipping name, ERG guide number, net weight, and the shipper's address
options.b: Identification number, proper shipping name, hazard class/division, and packing group
options.c: Identification number, trade name, hazard class, and the 24-hour emergency phone number
options.d: Packing group, hazard class, quantity, and number of packages in that order

distractorExplanations.a: ERG guide numbers and addresses are not part of the basic description, which is ID number, name, class and packing group.
distractorExplanations.c: The basic description uses the proper shipping name, not a trade name; the emergency phone is a separate required entry.
distractorExplanations.d: Quantity and package count are additional entries; the basic description sequence starts with the ID number and proper shipping name.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-classes-placa.explanation: The basic description sequence is standardized for clarity in emergencies. Packing group is shown when one is assigned.

options.a: Least danger
options.b: Medium danger
options.c: Great danger
options.d: Explosive risk

distractorExplanations.b: Medium danger is Packing Group II; Packing Group I indicates great danger, the highest of the three groups.
distractorExplanations.d: Explosives are Class 1 and use compatibility groups rather than packing groups; PG I means the greatest degree of danger.
distractorExplanations.a: PG III is lesser danger.

options.a: Class 2 (e.g., 2.1 flammable gases)
options.b: Class 3 (e.g., flammable liquids)
options.c: Class 5 (e.g., 5.1 oxidizers)
options.d: Class 4 (e.g., 4.1 flammable solids)

distractorExplanations.a: Division 2.1 covers flammable gases; flammable solids are classed in Division 4.1.
distractorExplanations.b: Class 3 is flammable liquids; flammable solids are Division 4.1 within Class 4.
distractorExplanations.c: Division 5.1 is oxidizers, which support combustion but are not flammable solids; those are Division 4.1.

options.a: A hazard warning label for the packaged hazmat
options.b: A placard required on the vehicle carrying it
options.c: A handling mark showing which side goes up
options.d: An ERG guide number for responders

distractorExplanations.b: Placards go on vehicles and bulk packages; the smaller diamond on a non-bulk package is a hazard label.
distractorExplanations.c: Orientation is shown by arrow marks, not a diamond; the square-on-point symbol is a hazard warning label.
distractorExplanations.d: ERG guide numbers appear in the guidebook, not on packages; the diamond on a package is the hazard label for its class.

options.a: Segregated according to segregation tables
options.b: Loaded together if each package is undamaged
options.c: Kept 12 inches apart in the cargo area
options.d: Placed in the order listed on the shipping papers

distractorExplanations.b: Intact packaging does not override segregation; the table forbids or restricts certain classes on one vehicle.
distractorExplanations.c: Segregation follows the 49 CFR 177.848 table codes (X, O, *); a fixed 12-inch gap is not the rule.
distractorExplanations.d: Shipping-paper order has no bearing on compatibility; the segregation table decides which classes may share a vehicle.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-loading-segre.explanation: Segregation prevents dangerous interactions (e.g., acids with cyanides) This keeps them from reacting dangerously if released.

options.a: Use hooks on drums to speed handling of heavy packages
options.b: Protect packages from damage and secure them against movement
options.c: Lay liquid packages on their side to lower the stack
options.d: Secure them after the trip begins, once the load has settled in place

distractorExplanations.a: Hooks and similar tools can puncture packages; loading rules bar tools that may damage hazmat containers.
distractorExplanations.c: Orientation arrows must be followed; laying liquid packages on their side can stress closures and cause leaks.
distractorExplanations.d: Packages must be secured against movement before the vehicle moves; loads that shift in transit can be damaged and leak.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-loading-segre.explanation: Package integrity and securement prevent leaks and incidents. Follow orientation marks as well.

options.a: Heaters drain the air system needed for the trailer brakes
options.b: Heated cargo areas require a separate placard
options.c: Heat/ignition sources can trigger fire or explosion
options.d: Heat raises the packing group of every material

distractorExplanations.a: Cargo heater limits are about ignition, not air supply; restrictions apply when hauling explosives and flammable liquids or gases.
distractorExplanations.b: No extra placard exists for heated cargo areas; heaters are restricted because they can ignite flammables or explosives.
distractorExplanations.d: Packing group is assigned at classification and does not change with temperature; heaters are restricted for ignition risk.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-loading-segre.explanation: Ignition control is critical near flammables and explosives. This matters most with flammables and explosives.

options.a: Whether the package is placarded
options.b: The hazard class and packing group of the contents
options.c: Whether the shipment needs an emergency phone number
options.d: Capacity thresholds defined in the HMR

distractorExplanations.a: Placarding follows from what is shipped, but bulk vs non-bulk is defined by capacity (e.g., over 119 gallons for liquids).
distractorExplanations.b: Class and packing group describe the hazard; bulk status depends on the package's capacity thresholds.
distractorExplanations.c: An emergency response phone is needed for most hazmat shipments either way; bulk vs non-bulk depends on capacity.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-loading-segre.explanation: HMR define bulk vs non-bulk by volume/weight capacity criteria. Bulk packages generally have the larger capacities.

options.a: The vehicle is appropriate, free of ignition hazards
options.b: The cargo floor has exposed metal to ground static charges
options.c: The cargo heater is running to keep detonators dry
options.d: Blasting caps are loaded with Division 1.1 explosives

distractorExplanations.b: For Class 1, the cargo floor must be tight and lined with non-metallic or non-ferrous material, not bare metal that can spark.
distractorExplanations.c: Cargo heaters are restricted with explosives because they are ignition sources; they must be off or made inoperable.
distractorExplanations.d: Detonators may not ride with Division 1.1 explosives unless packed in approved containers under the segregation rules.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-loading-segre.explanation: Explosives demand strict fire control and compliance. Loading must follow quantity and segregation rules.

options.a: Coated with oil so heavy drums slide into their position easily
options.b: Clean and free of nails/screws that could puncture packages
options.c: Lined with loose straw to cushion every package
options.d: Free of leaks, with nails left for tying off straps

distractorExplanations.a: A slick or contaminated floor lets packages shift and can react with cargo; it must be clean and dry.
distractorExplanations.c: Loose combustible dunnage adds fire load; the requirement is a clean floor free of projections, plus proper securement.
distractorExplanations.d: Protruding nails and screws can puncture packages; they must be removed or made flush, not used as tie points.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-loading-segre.explanation: Puncture and contamination risks must be controlled before loading. The floor must also be in good condition.

options.a: Left slightly open to vent vapor pressure during transit
options.b: Closed once the tank is emptied at delivery
options.c: Closed by the loader, with no driver check needed
options.d: Closed and secured per procedures; check for leaks

distractorExplanations.a: Manholes and valves must be closed during transit; venting is handled by the tank's pressure-relief devices, not open covers.
distractorExplanations.b: Covers and valves are closed before the loaded tank moves, not just after unloading; open covers spill product en route.
distractorExplanations.c: The driver must verify that manholes and valves are closed and leak-free before moving a loaded cargo tank.

options.a: Away from foodstuffs and per segregation/separation rules
options.b: With foodstuffs if each package is sealed and fully intact
options.c: In the cab where the driver can watch for leaks
options.d: Near the rear doors so fumes vent while driving

distractorExplanations.b: Division 6.1 materials may not ride with foodstuffs unless separated as 49 CFR 177.841 requires, however intact the packages look.
distractorExplanations.c: Toxic materials must not ride in the driver's compartment; they belong in the cargo area away from food and people.
distractorExplanations.d: Packages stay closed and secured; placing them to vent implies leakage, and leaking toxic packages must not be transported.

options.a: Loaded if the leak is wiped and taped shut
options.b: Not loaded; protect people and notify appropriate parties
options.c: Loaded upright with absorbent material packed around its base
options.d: Loaded, then reported to the shipper on arrival

distractorExplanations.a: Leaking packages may not be accepted for transport; a temporary patch does not make them fit to ship.
distractorExplanations.c: Absorbent helps clean up but does not make a leaking package acceptable; it must be refused and reported.
distractorExplanations.d: The package must not be loaded at all; notification happens at the dock before any transport.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-loading-segre.explanation: Do not accept damaged/leaking packages; follow emergency and carrier procedures. Contain the leak only if trained and safe.

options.a: Slowing to 15 mph and looking both ways without stopping
options.b: Stopping within 10 feet of the nearest rail, then crossing in the highest gear
options.c: Stopping (with exceptions) before crossing, listening, and proceeding only when safe
options.d: Stopping 15 to 50 feet before, then shifting gears while on the tracks

distractorExplanations.a: Placarded vehicles must stop 15 to 50 feet before the nearest rail; slowing without stopping does not meet the rule.
distractorExplanations.b: The stop is 15 to 50 feet from the nearest rail, and the driver uses a gear that avoids shifting; 10 feet is too close.
distractorExplanations.d: The stop distance is right, but shifting gears while crossing is prohibited; select a gear that lets you cross without shifting.

options.a: Loose cylinders only matter when they are full of flammable gas
options.b: Loose cylinders are acceptable if their valve caps are in place
options.c: Segregation applies to gas cylinders in cargo tanks but not inside dry vans
options.d: Damaged valves/releases can create fire, asphyxiation, or toxic exposure

distractorExplanations.a: Nonflammable gases can still asphyxiate, and oxidizers or toxics create other hazards; every cylinder must be secured.
distractorExplanations.b: Valve caps protect valves, but cylinders must still be secured upright or braced and segregated; caps alone are not enough.
distractorExplanations.c: The segregation table applies to packages on any transport vehicle, including cylinders loaded in vans and flatbeds.

options.a: Keep package upright as marked
options.b: Stack two high at most
options.c: Load this end toward the trailer front
options.d: Handle with care; contents are fragile

distractorExplanations.b: Stacking limits are shown by a separate stacking mark; orientation arrows show which way up the package travels.
distractorExplanations.c: Arrows point up, not toward the front; they show the vertical orientation needed to keep closures from leaking.
distractorExplanations.d: Fragile handling uses a different mark; orientation arrows show the package must stay upright as marked.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-loading-segre.explanation: Liquid closures and vents may depend on upright orientation. Exceptions apply only where rules allow otherwise.

options.a: Shift weight enough to change the placards required
options.b: Void the shipping papers until the load is restacked
options.c: Damage packages, open closures, and cause spills
options.d: Raise the packing group of the materials on board

distractorExplanations.a: Placarding depends on what is aboard, not where it sits; movement matters because it can damage packages and cause leaks.
distractorExplanations.b: Shipping papers remain valid after shifting; the danger is package damage, open closures and releases.
distractorExplanations.d: Packing groups are fixed by the material's hazard; shifting cargo causes damage and spills, not reclassification.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-loading-segre.explanation: Load securement is a core prevention control. Released materials can also react dangerously.

options.a: Park away from people/ignition sources and notify emergency/carrier contacts
options.b: Drive on to the next truck stop to find help and absorbent
options.c: Locate the leak by smell to identify the material first
options.d: Park near a building so responders can find you quickly, and wait in the cab

distractorExplanations.b: Driving a leaking hazmat vehicle spreads contamination and can be illegal; park safely as soon as possible instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Smell or touch must not be used to identify hazmat; check the shipping papers and ERG from a safe distance.
distractorExplanations.d: Park away from people and buildings, and do not stay where vapors can reach you; then notify responders.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-driving-emerg.explanation: Protect life and limit ignition/exposure; use ERG/carrier emergency procedures. Secure the scene and keep people away.

options.a: Water on a tire fire reacts with every class of hazmat
options.b: Heat can involve the cargo and cause a larger fire
options.c: Tire fires require evacuation only for Class 1 loads
options.d: Tires on placarded vehicles are made of flammable compounds

distractorExplanations.a: Water is often used to cool tire fires; the danger is heat reaching the cargo, not a universal water reaction.
distractorExplanations.c: Heat from a tire fire can ignite or rupture many classes, including flammable liquids and gases, not just explosives.
distractorExplanations.d: Tires are the same on any truck; the extra danger is the hazardous cargo the fire can reach.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-driving-emerg.explanation: Stop/address tire issues early; cargo involvement escalates incidents. Cargo involvement can mean explosion or toxic release.

options.a: Decide whether the load still needs placards after a spill
options.b: Find the carrier's insurance and claims contact details
options.c: Identify material hazards and initial protective distances/actions
options.d: Choose the cleanup method and neutralizing chemicals to apply

distractorExplanations.a: Placarding is set before transport; in an emergency, papers and the ERG identify the material and initial protective actions.
distractorExplanations.b: Insurance details are not the purpose; papers and the ERG identify the material, its hazards and initial isolation distances.
distractorExplanations.d: Cleanup is for trained responders; the ERG gives initial isolation and protective actions, not driver cleanup procedures.

options.a: Warn others, set out emergency triangles as required, and call for assistance
options.b: Set out burning flares around the vehicle to warn traffic
options.c: Walk to the nearest exit for help, leaving the shipping papers on the driver's seat
options.d: Use four-way flashers in place of triangles until help arrives

distractorExplanations.b: Flame-producing flares may not be used near vehicles carrying explosives or flammable cargo; use reflective triangles.
distractorExplanations.c: The vehicle must not be left unprotected; call for help from the scene and keep it attended and warned.
distractorExplanations.d: Flashers are used while placing warning devices, but triangles are still required within 10 minutes of stopping.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-driving-emerg.explanation: Traffic control and notification reduce secondary crashes and exposures. Do not leave the scene unprotected.

options.a: Your carrier's name and USDOT number before any other details
options.b: The product's trade name and the shipper's billing address
options.c: Location, material identity/UN number, and injuries/hazards observed
options.d: The hazard class read off the placard, without checking the shipping papers

distractorExplanations.a: Carrier details help later, but responders first need location, material identity and injuries to plan the response.
distractorExplanations.b: Trade names and billing details do not tell responders the hazard; give the proper shipping name or UN number.
distractorExplanations.d: Placards show only the class; shipping papers give the exact material and UN number and should be checked when safe.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-driving-emerg.explanation: Accurate identity and location enable correct response. Quantity and conditions also help responders.

options.a: Rely on standard fire gear without breathing apparatus
options.b: Use the general orange-page isolation instead of the green table
options.c: Approach from downwind to see the vapor cloud
options.d: Emphasize respiratory protection and isolation downwind

distractorExplanations.a: TIH materials injure through inhalation; turnout gear alone is not enough, so respiratory protection is emphasized.
distractorExplanations.b: TIH materials are listed in the ERG green table for isolation and protective-action distances beyond the orange-page guidance.
distractorExplanations.c: Responders approach from upwind; approaching from downwind puts them in the vapor path of an inhalation hazard.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-driving-emerg.explanation: TIH materials demand atmospheric precautions; follow ERG/specialist advice. Follow ERG guidance.

options.a: Apply water inappropriately, generating flammable/toxic gases
options.b: Smother the fire with dry sand or a Class D agent
options.c: Let the fire burn while keeping people at a distance
options.d: Cover the spill with a dry plastic sheet to keep rain off

distractorExplanations.b: Dry sand or special dry agents are typical recommended methods for water-reactive materials; they do not worsen the fire.
distractorExplanations.c: Isolating the area and letting responders choose the method is a protective action; it does not generate reactive gases.
distractorExplanations.d: Keeping water away from a Division 4.3 material is a recommended ERG step; keeping it dry helps rather than worsens.

options.a: Wipe the skin with gasoline to dissolve the diesel
options.b: Remove contaminated clothing and wash skin with soap/water
options.c: Leave the clothing on and rinse it later at the hotel
options.d: Rinse only with water; soap spreads the fuel

distractorExplanations.a: Solvents like gasoline irritate skin and increase absorption; soap and water is the standard first wash.
distractorExplanations.c: Diesel-soaked clothing keeps fuel against the skin; contaminated clothing is removed promptly and the skin washed.
distractorExplanations.d: Soap and water remove oily fuel more effectively; soap does not spread diesel on the skin.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-driving-emerg.explanation: Decontaminate skin; avoid absurd harmful 'remedies' Seek care if irritation persists.

options.a: Steer hazmat trucks onto the shortest available route to cut their exposure time
options.b: Keep hazmat trucks off interstates and on local roads
options.c: Keep high-risk loads away from tunnels, bridges, or densely populated routes
options.d: Spread hazmat traffic evenly so no single route carries too much

distractorExplanations.a: Routing rules can require a longer designated route; the shortest path may pass through restricted tunnels or cities.
distractorExplanations.b: Preferred routes usually favor interstates and bypasses; local roads through towns are what routing rules try to avoid.
distractorExplanations.d: Routing restrictions keep high-risk materials away from tunnels, bridges and populated areas; they do not spread traffic.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-driving-emerg.explanation: Follow designated/preferred routes and prohibitions for the material and jurisdiction. Follow designated or preferred routes as required.

options.a: Go by the placards, since they are checked at loading
options.b: Correct the shipping papers yourself to match the placards
options.c: Deliver the load and report the mismatch on arrival
options.d: Not move the shipment until discrepancies are resolved

distractorExplanations.a: Shipping papers and placards must agree; neither is assumed correct, so the load waits until the discrepancy is resolved.
distractorExplanations.b: The shipper certifies the papers; the driver does not rewrite them but contacts the shipper/carrier to resolve the mismatch.
distractorExplanations.c: Transport should not continue with conflicting hazard information; resolve the discrepancy before moving.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-driving-emerg.explanation: Identification must be accurate before transport continues. Use shipper/carrier procedures to resolve it.

options.a: Available for the materials transported
options.b: Kept at the carrier's dispatch office
options.c: Provided only for Class 1 and Class 7 loads
options.d: Posted on the vehicle beside the placards

distractorExplanations.b: Emergency response information must travel with the shipment and be immediately accessible to the driver and responders.
distractorExplanations.c: Emergency response information is required for most hazmat shipments that need shipping papers, not just explosives and radioactives.
distractorExplanations.d: Emergency information stays with the shipping papers in the cab; the vehicle exterior carries placards, not response guidance.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-driving-emerg.explanation: Emergency response information is required to accompany hazmat shipments. ERG pages or equivalent emergency information qualify.

options.a: Move people downwind where the air is clearer
options.b: Move people upwind and keep them away from vapors
options.c: Move people downhill, away from the spill site
options.d: Gather everyone close to the vehicle to keep a headcount

distractorExplanations.a: Downwind is the direction vapors travel; evacuate people upwind and uphill of the release.
distractorExplanations.c: Heavier-than-air vapors flow downhill; move people upwind and uphill, not downhill.
distractorExplanations.d: Staying near the vehicle keeps people in the hazard zone; move them to a safe distance upwind before counting.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-driving-emerg.explanation: Protect by distance, wind direction, and denying entry. Use guidance distances to decide how far.

options.a: Move the package to the cab to keep it under watch
options.b: Wrap it in plastic and reload it away from people
options.c: Minimize time near the package, maximize distance/shielding
options.d: Continue the trip because the package label shows Radioactive White-I

distractorExplanations.a: Bringing it closer increases exposure; time, distance and shielding mean staying away and isolating the area.
distractorExplanations.b: Handling a damaged radioactive package adds exposure and spreads contamination; isolate it and wait for qualified help.
distractorExplanations.d: White-I means low surface radiation for an intact package; a damaged package needs isolation and notification.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-driving-emerg.explanation: Time-distance-shielding and expert response apply to radiological concerns. Isolate the area and notify authorities and the carrier.

options.a: Recognize and reduce security risks
options.b: Classify materials and select placards
options.c: Respond to spills using the ERG
options.d: Pass the TSA background check

distractorExplanations.b: Classification and placarding are covered by function-specific training; security awareness targets threats like theft and tampering.
distractorExplanations.c: Emergency response training covers spills; security awareness training is about recognizing and responding to security threats.
distractorExplanations.d: The TSA threat assessment is for the HME driver; security awareness training is required for every hazmat employee.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-security-rule.explanation: Security plans/awareness reduce intentional misuse of hazardous materials. Risks include theft, tampering, or terrorism targeting hazmat.

options.a: Asking them to leave and taking no further action
options.b: Reporting to security/law enforcement per site procedures
options.c: Confronting them and seizing the camera yourself
options.d: Waiting to see whether they come back a second or third time

distractorExplanations.a: Unusual surveillance of a hazmat site should be reported; just sending the person away loses information security needs.
distractorExplanations.c: Employees should avoid confrontation; the correct step is to note details and report to security or police.
distractorExplanations.d: Suspicious activity is reported promptly; waiting for repeat visits gives a possible attacker more time.

options.a: A placard showing the high-risk status on the vehicle
options.b: Sharing route details with any caller who asks for them
options.c: Enhanced security plans and route/communication practices
options.d: Using any route as long as the shipment is placarded

distractorExplanations.a: Placards are hazard communication for every placarded load; they are not an added security measure for high-risk materials.
distractorExplanations.b: Route and schedule information is protected under a security plan and shared on a need-to-know basis.
distractorExplanations.d: High-risk materials may require designated routes and route planning; placarding does not permit any route.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-security-rule.explanation: Higher-risk materials trigger stronger security plan requirements. Attendance and securement rules also apply as required.

options.a: Parking at isolated rest areas overnight to stay out of public sight
options.b: Leaving the engine running when stepping out briefly
options.c: Sharing route plans on the CB to get traffic updates
options.d: Minimizing stops, locking vehicles, and being aware of tailing

distractorExplanations.a: Isolated spots invite theft or hijacking; secure, well-lit, attended locations are preferred.
distractorExplanations.b: A running, unlocked truck is an easy theft target; lock the vehicle and take the keys at every stop.
distractorExplanations.c: Broadcasting routes and load details gives would-be attackers information; keep route details need-to-know.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-security-rule.explanation: Reduce opportunities for theft/hijack of hazmat. Watch for tampering as well.

options.a: Possible tampering—follow company procedures and report
options.b: A routine seal failure from road vibration
options.c: A shipper error to fix by resealing and going on
options.d: Nothing to report if the placards are still in place

distractorExplanations.b: Seals rarely break from vibration; an unexpected broken seal is treated as possible tampering until checked.
distractorExplanations.c: Resealing without reporting hides possible tampering; follow company procedures and report before continuing.
distractorExplanations.d: Placards say nothing about cargo access; a broken seal signals possible tampering that must be reported.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-security-rule.explanation: Seal integrity is a security control; anomalies need response. Document it before proceeding.

options.a: A knowledge test and a clean driving record for 3 years
options.b: TSA security threat assessment plus knowledge testing
options.c: A skills test in a placarded vehicle plus a medical card
options.d: Carrier hazmat training records instead of a CDL test

distractorExplanations.a: A clean record is not the requirement; the HME needs a TSA security threat assessment with fingerprints plus the knowledge test.
distractorExplanations.c: There is no hazmat skills test; the endorsement requires the hazmat knowledge test and the TSA threat assessment.
distractorExplanations.d: Employer training is required separately but does not replace the hazmat knowledge test and TSA assessment.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-security-rule.explanation: Federal security threat assessment is part of hazmat endorsement issuance. The TSA process includes fingerprint-based background checks.

options.a: Police have already opened an investigation
options.b: Only after a second suspicious visit by the same person at the counter
options.c: Behavior suggests planning to misuse hazardous materials
options.d: A manager confirms the buyer is not a regular customer

distractorExplanations.a: Reporting should not wait for an official investigation; employees report when behavior suggests planned misuse.
distractorExplanations.b: Waiting for repeat visits delays a report that could prevent an attack; report as soon as behavior seems suspicious.
distractorExplanations.d: Reporting depends on suspicious behavior, not customer status; regular customers can also show signs of planned misuse.

options.a: Open to any employee of the facility during work hours
options.b: Unlocked during the day when staff are on site
options.c: Granted to drivers who show a valid CDL
options.d: Limited to authorized personnel with controls

distractorExplanations.a: Access is limited to authorized personnel with a need to enter, not every employee on shift.
distractorExplanations.b: Being staffed does not control access; storage areas stay locked or badge-controlled during working hours too.
distractorExplanations.c: A CDL does not authorize entry to storage areas; access depends on authorization and site controls.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-security-rule.explanation: Physical access control is a core security measure. Controls include locks, badges, and escorts as required.

options.a: The driver must stay inside the cab at all times
options.b: Someone qualified may need to attend the vehicle
options.c: A locked vehicle counts as attended for Class 1
options.d: The driver may watch it from a sleeper berth

distractorExplanations.a: Attendance means being awake, not in the sleeper berth, within 100 feet and with a clear view of the vehicle; staying in the cab is not required.
distractorExplanations.c: Division 1.1–1.3 vehicles must be attended by a qualified person; locking the vehicle does not meet the rule unless it is on a safe haven.
distractorExplanations.d: A person in the sleeper berth is not attending; the attendant must be awake and within 100 feet with the vehicle in view.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-security-rule.explanation: Attendance/surveillance rules reduce theft and unauthorized access—know the material-specific requirements. The specific rule set may require keeping it within view.

options.a: Pull over on the shoulder and let the vehicle pass
options.b: Speed up and take back roads to lose the follower
options.c: Avoid confrontation, note details, and contact law enforcement
options.d: Drive straight on to the receiver and report it once the delivery is done

distractorExplanations.a: Stopping on a shoulder makes the truck an easy target; keep moving toward a safe, populated area while reporting.
distractorExplanations.b: Evasive driving with hazmat raises crash risk and can lead into isolated areas; stay on route and contact police.
distractorExplanations.d: Hostile surveillance is reported right away to police or carrier security, not after the delivery is complete.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-security-rule.explanation: Personal safety and reporting beat vigilantism. Carrier security should also be contacted per procedure.

options.a: Physically stopping entry to the cargo area
options.b: Replacing the need for padlocks on high-risk hazmat loads
options.c: Recording who opened the trailer and when it happened
options.d: Showing whether unauthorized access to cargo may have occurred

distractorExplanations.a: Seals are not barriers; they show evidence of access, while locks are what physically resist entry.
distractorExplanations.b: Tamper-evident seals complement locks rather than replace them; they reveal intrusion but do not prevent it.
distractorExplanations.c: A basic seal shows only that access may have occurred; it does not log identities or times like an electronic lock.

options.a: Personnel security, unauthorized access, and en-route security measures
options.b: Spill response steps, ERG isolation distances, and first-aid procedures
options.c: Placarding, package labeling, and shipping paper accuracy checks
options.d: Driver hours of service, logbook audits, and required rest breaks

distractorExplanations.b: Spill response belongs to emergency response planning; a security plan covers personnel, access and en-route security.
distractorExplanations.c: Hazard communication rules cover papers and placards; the security plan addresses theft and misuse risks.
distractorExplanations.d: HOS rules are separate FMCSA requirements; security plans focus on personnel checks, access control and en-route security.

options.a: Acceptable if the person rides in the cab only
options.b: A serious security and safety violation
options.c: A minor issue unless the load is Class 1
options.d: Permitted if the passenger has a CDL

distractorExplanations.a: Unauthorized passengers are not allowed in a CMV even in the cab; carrier authorization is required under 49 CFR 392.60.
distractorExplanations.c: Unauthorized access is a serious violation for any hazmat load, not just explosives.
distractorExplanations.d: Holding a CDL does not authorize someone to ride along or enter the cargo area; carrier authorization is required.

options.a: Drop the trailer at the gate if the receiver is closed
options.b: Hand over the load to anyone signing the bill of lading
options.c: Verify receiver authorization and document exceptions
options.d: Remove placards before arrival to stay inconspicuous

distractorExplanations.a: Leaving a loaded hazmat trailer unattended at a closed site invites theft; follow carrier instructions for secure parking.
distractorExplanations.b: A signature alone does not prove authorization; verify the receiver's identity and authorization before handing over.
distractorExplanations.d: Placards must stay on while hazmat is aboard; removing them breaks hazard communication rules and does not improve security.

cdl-hazmat-readiness-check-security-rule.explanation: Identity verification and documentation prevent diversion. Check seals and IDs per procedure.
